claims.text: Ethanol oxidation activity, selectivity, and durability in Pt or Pt-Sn alloy nanoparticles are governed by controlled sub-monolayer surface oxide patches.
Sub-monolayer oxide patches facilitate water activation and the generation of surface OH groups.
OH-generating oxide patches adjacent to metallic ethanol-adsorption sites enable a bifunctional ethanol-oxidation mechanism.
The proposed bifunctional mechanism promotes the 12-electron oxidation of ethanol to CO2.
Excessive oxide coverage causes deactivation through bulk oxidation.
Cycling between 0.0 and 0.7 V versus RHE will induce moderate sub-monolayer oxide formation.
In Pt-Sn catalysts, the relevant structural mediator may take the form of mixed-valence oxide domains coexisting with adjacent metallic sites.
Oxide-derived OH groups facilitate oxidative dehydrogenation of ethanol adsorbed on neighboring metallic sites.
Oxide coverage has an optimum, above which activity and durability decrease.
Moderate oxide coverage produced by the pre-treatment will increase current density relative to untreated catalysts.
Moderate oxide coverage produced by the pre-treatment will increase selectivity toward CO2 relative to untreated catalysts.
Moderate oxide coverage produced by the pre-treatment will improve catalyst durability relative to untreated catalysts.
Both under-oxidation and over-oxidation will diminish ethanol-oxidation performance.
The proposed mechanism applies in acidic electrolyte at room temperature under potential cycling that permits controlled oxide formation.
The proposed mechanism may fail when oxide formation is prevented or when high potentials or different pH conditions cause excessive bulk oxidation.
Support modifications and other factors may confound the correlation between oxide coverage and catalytic performance.
